Sample proportion p̂ = 12/80 = 0.15.

rounds.response: If you do not reject H0 and the 95% CI includes 0.25 but is wide, you have insufficient evidence to conclude the true proportion differs from 0.25 — it’s inconclusive, not proof that p = 0.25. The wide CI quantifies uncertainty: it shows the range of plausible p values, so check whether values that would be practically important lie inside that interval. Statistical significance answers whether the data rule out H0 at α; practical significance asks whether the effect sizes in the CI are large enough to matter in context. If the CI still contains clinically/managerially important differences, the result may be practically important even though it’s not statistically significant; consider increasing sample size or reporting a power analysis targeted at the minimally important difference. Always report the CI and discuss both statistical and practical implications rather than relying only on the p-value.

Single-proportion z-test: state H0: p = p0 and Ha (one- or two-sided); check np0 and n(1−p0) ≥ 10; SE0 = sqrt[p0(1−p0)/n]; z = (p̂−p0)/SE0, get p-value and compare to α to decide.  
Two independent proportions: compute p̂1,p̂2; CI: SE = sqrt[p̂1(1−p̂1)/n1 + p̂2(1−p̂2)/n2], CI = (p̂1−p̂2) ± z*SE; two-sample z-test (H0: p1=p2) use pooled p̂ = (x1+x2)/(n1+n2) with SE0 = sqrt[p̂(1−p̂)(1/n1+1/n2)), z = (p̂1−p̂2)/SE0; always check independence and ≥10 successes and ≥10 failures per group and use Wilson/exact methods if counts are small or proportions near 0 or 1.
